theme_note: Participants organize when the reversal begins and ends, who may join, and how the act should be performed; the codes vary between timing, permission, voice, and limits on conduct.
Participants perform the reversal rather than merely mention it, using declarations, binary, software talk, greetings, disguises, and mock hostility.

second_order: revealing the robot act as the April Fool
theme_note: Participants explain, expose, or justify a robot performance by naming April first, the day's joke, the proposal, or time-zone timing; some reveal their own act and others explain someone else's.

second_order: correcting and challenging one another's performance
theme_note: Participants make the bit answerable by objecting, coaching, invoking rules, correcting speech or code, and accusing others of being unconvincing; what varies is whether the repair is social, calendrical, linguistic, or technical.

second_order: carrying the in-joke beyond its starting thread
theme_note: Participants point the performance outward or bring an outside instance back; the destinations and degree of visible return vary.

second_order: recasting ordinary life as robot activity
theme_note: Participants press food, sleep, bodies, breathing, care, and other ordinary acts into the room's machine register.

second_order: keeping the shared laugh running in code
theme_note: A long exchange sustains laughter by programming, rating, breaking, explaining, and finally ending it; the variation is in languages, number jokes, and whether the loop is prolonged or stopped.

second_order: testing who can pass as human
theme_note: Participants treat speech, code, mistakes, denials, and nested impersonation as tests of humanity; this differs from simply acting as a robot because these turns judge or prove who someone is.

second_order: writing rules for how to be human
theme_note: Participants collaboratively supply a manual for seeming human, varying from bodies and loud speech to repeated denials and a quick guide for passing.

second_order: having moderation join and name the takeover
theme_note: The subreddit frames moderation as powered down, then a moderator powers up, accepts robotic status, and calls the move a prank.

second_order: building a CAPTCHA to prove they are human
theme_note: Participants turn the room's proof-of-humanity joke into canvas work by proposing an image, supplying coordinates, clicking, scripting, recruiting, and disputing whether proof is needed or inclusive.

Participants negotiate where the CAPTCHA can fit by identifying the Patriots scoreboard, proposing smaller or alternate placements, and refusing to cover flags; positions vary between accommodation and displacement.

second_order: moving the display before time runs out
theme_note: As the first placement falters, participants struggle to start an arrow, issue an emergency relocation and new coordinates, and console the organizer that it was too late.

second_order: closing, mourning, and checking the failed display
theme_note: After placement stops, participants declare failure, mourn what was unfinished, explain the project, close it civilly, express relief, admit uneven awareness, and dispute whether anything survived in the final collage.

second_order: playing along with the deleted painting post
theme_note: The surviving title and replies present a painting, answer it in binary, and ask where Wally is; the missing body prevents joining this small practice to the CAPTCHA work.

second_order: answering r/foxes over the damaged fox
theme_note: A fox visitor asks for diplomacy and later accuses the community of ruining the fox; replies range from assimilation wordplay to an apology on the community's behalf.

second_order: inviting humans to continue on PlaceTwo
theme_note: A single post invites the proof-of-humanity display onto another canvas; no visible response lets it join a collective continuation practice.
